newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief approves Iraqi food plan, Iraq to pump oil.
newsitem.headline: UN chief approves Iraqi food plan, Iraq to pump oil.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Monday approved an Iraqi distribution plan for food, medicine and other supplies, necessary before Baghdad would agree to resume oil exports.
In response, Iraq's U.N. ambassador, Nizar Hamdoon, told Reuters he anticipated no delays in implementing plans to begin pumping oil again.
The next step would be for Iraq to submit an oil pricing formula, which U.N. overseers or oil experts have to approve. He said Baghdad expected to submit the plan "very soon."
At issue is a 680-page plan in which Iraq has outlined how it will distribute goods bought under an oil-for-food programme that went into effect last December and was renewed in June.

This plan allows Iraq to sell up to $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food, medicine and other supplies for its people under U.N. sanctions in force since Baghdad's troops invaded Kuwait in 1990.

Iraq had tied the resumption of exports to approval from Annan of the distribution plan, apparently to make sure the United States and other council members quickly endorse contracts for food, medicine and other goods.
Oil sales have been divided into two 90-day periods. The plan was renewed for another 180 days or six months on June 8.
Iraq had maintained that the startup date for the latest phase of the plan would begin when Annan approved the programme.
But the Council two weeks ago insisted the day was still June 8. So Iraq will have just over a month to try to meet its sales quota before the first 90-day period expires on Sept. 5.

"The secretary-general sent to the president of the Security Council a letter informing the council that (he) had approved Iraq's plan for the purchase and distribution of human supplies under the oil-for-food programme," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said.
In answer to questions, he said,"The terms are that there can be no change in the time from for the sales. So they have just a matter of weeks instead of the full three months."
"I expect they will be pumping at maximum capacity as soon as possible, he added.

Oil cannot flow freely, however, until the sanctions are lifted. One key requirement for lifting the ban on oil exports is a clean bill of health from U.N. arms inspectors that Iraq has destroyed its weapons of mass destruction, related material and plans.

One obstacle that delayed approval was Iraq's reported failure to earmark goods for the most vulnerable, such as handicapped children and the sick. Eckhard said last week the U.N. believed it had settled the issue and received assurances from Iraq "in writing."
Eckhard also announced that Denis Halliday of Ireland had been appointed as the new humanitarian coordinator for the programme, in which more than 100 U.N. monitors are supervising the deal.

Halliday, an assistant secretary-general in charge of personnel, will replace Staffan de Mistura of Italy, a veteran U.N. relief assistance official, who went to Iraq in February. A new head of personnel will be named.
